title: Ephesians
subtitle: One new people, chosen before the world began
lead: Ephesians is a letter that begins by praising God in a single breath and ends by calling its readers to stand firm against hostile powers. In between it tells what God has done in Christ: chosen a people before the world was made, adopted and redeemed them, raised them from death by grace, and made Jews and Gentiles one new humanity, a household and a holy temple. Its great theme is a secret kept hidden for ages and now made known: that God's plan is to bring everything in heaven and on earth together in Christ, and that the church, made of Jews and Gentiles together, is where that plan can already be seen.

The letter names Paul as its author and has been read as his since the second century. Many modern scholars think it was written after Paul's death by a follower; many others defend Paul as the author. It is also unclear who the first readers were, since the words 'in Ephesus' are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts. This Plain English Translation translation follows the text and presents the questions fairly. The letter is much the same whichever answer you prefer, and it has shaped Christian teaching on election, grace, the church, marriage and spiritual conflict.
facts: Traditionally Paul (1:1; 3:1). Many scholars hold that it was written in his name by a follower after his death; many others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps through a secretary or co-worker. See the authorship table.
If Paul wrote it, about AD 62 from Rome (Caesarea and Ephesus have also been proposed). If a follower wrote it, about AD 70-100.
Paul is a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). The place is not named; Rome, Caesarea and Ephesus have all been proposed.
Gentile Christians (2:11; 3:1) in Ephesus or in a group of churches in the Roman province of Asia (modern western Turkey). Some of the oldest manuscripts have no city named in 1:1.

A letter in the shape of a blessing, a report of prayer, a doctrinal teaching, a second prayer and doxology (chapters 1-3), then instruction in daily life (chapters 4-6). It lacks the personal greetings and arguments of Paul's letters to churches he knew.
Greek, with many long sentences. The first sentence, 1:3-14, has 202 words in the Greek text used here.
authorship: It begins with 'Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God' (1:1), speaks of 'I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus' (3:1) and sends Tychicus with news (6:21-22). Nothing in the letter says that it was written by anyone else.

From the second century the church took the letter as Paul's. Polycarp's letter to the Philippians echoes 2:8-9 and perhaps cites 4:26 in the words 'It is declared then in these Scriptures, Be angry, and sin not' (Polycarp 1:3; 12:1, in the Roberts-Donaldson translation); Irenaeus cites it as Paul's; Tertullian knows it as 'to the Ephesians' and accuses Marcion of changing the title; the Muratorian list names it among Paul's letters. The case for Paul today is made by Hoehner, Arnold, Thielman and Barth, among others. Defenders say that Paul as a prisoner and in a different setting would write in a different style, that a secretary or co-worker could shape it, and that the many links with Colossians are explained by two letters written within weeks of each other and carried by the same man (Tychicus, Colossians 4:7-9; Ephesians 6:21-22).

Since the 1800s many scholars have doubted that Paul wrote it. Lincoln, Best and Schnackenburg hold that it was written by a disciple after Paul's death. Reasons given by those who doubt Paul's authorship: the very long sentences and a lot of vocabulary and phrases found nowhere else in Paul; a close dependence on Colossians; a view of the church as a universal body with Christ as head; the stress that salvation is already complete (2:5-6); 'holy apostles and prophets' as the foundation of the church (2:20; 3:5); the settled tone and the lack of personal greetings, strange from a man who lived among these readers for three years; and a view of Paul as the great apostle of the mystery (3:1-13).

Writing in a teacher's name was known in the ancient world and its morals were disputed. Paul himself warns of letters falsely claimed to come from him and marks his own hand (2 Thessalonians 2:2; 3:17), and the Muratorian list rejects letters forged in Paul's name, among them one 'to the Laodiceans' and one 'to the Alexandrians'. Tertullian reports that an Asian presbyter who composed the Acts of Paul 'out of love for Paul' was removed from office (On Baptism 17); that work is a story, not a letter, but it shows the church's concern. Defenders of a disciple's authorship say the practice was a loving continuation of a teacher's voice; critics say it was a deception, and a letter that claims 'I, Paul' in the first person cannot be that. The question of honesty is part of the debate, and both sides take it seriously.

Some propose that Paul gave the outline and a co-worker wrote the letter, which Paul approved. Edgar Goodspeed suggested that Ephesians was written as a covering letter for the first collection of Paul's letters, perhaps by Onesimus (compare Philemon). Goodspeed and C. L. Mitton are among the scholars who doubt that Paul wrote it. None of these theories has been generally accepted.

The Plain English Translation follows the text, which names Paul as the writer; the book page says 'traditionally Paul' and labels the question. The notes say 'Paul' and, where it matters, set out the view that a disciple wrote it. Nothing in the translation depends on the choice.

audience.to: Gentile Christians (2:11; 3:1) in Ephesus, or in a group of churches in the Roman province of Asia, of whom some might never have met Paul. The make-up of the readers is clear in one respect: they were mostly non-Jews who had come to Christ out of the worship of many gods, in a region of powerful temples, magic and emperor worship. Jewish believers are part of the picture as the 'we' of 1:3-12 and the 'both' of 2:14-18, but the letter speaks to Gentiles. The first readers had heard of Paul's work (3:2; 4:21) and might know his name more than his face. If a large city church is meant, it was the center of a region where Paul had taught for three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31), and it would have included Gentiles who were once God-fearers at the synagogue and Gentiles who had worshiped Artemis.
audience.why: The letter does not answer a crisis as Galatians, 1 Corinthians or Colossians do. It reads as an encouragement and a teaching to Gentile believers who needed to know where they stood: in God's plan from before the world, in a people that took in Jews and Gentiles, and in a power that is greater than the powers they once feared. Since the second half asks for unity (4:1-6), a life different from the old pagan life (4:17-5:20), orderly households (5:21-6:9) and endurance against evil (6:10-20), the letter appears to be a teaching of how to live as a new people. How knowing the audience changes the reading: the Gentile readers hear 2:11-22 as a welcome and as a warning not to forget what they were; Jewish readers, then and now, may hear it as an account of how others were admitted to a household that was already theirs.
views: The words 'in Ephesus' are original, and the letter went first to the church there and then to others near it. The general tone, with no personal greetings, is explained by Paul writing to a church he knew well, with a message to be shared.

The letter was meant for several churches of Asia, with a blank for the name that each copy filled in. This view is widely held; Colossians 4:16 mentions a letter 'from Laodicea' that might be this one.

Marcion's collection knew a letter 'to the Laodiceans' (Tertullian, Against Marcion 5.11, 5.17), which some take to be this one. Tertullian says the church's title was 'to the Ephesians'. Whether Marcion's title was a guess, a different letter or an old title is unknown.
A general letter by a disciple
The letter was written after Paul's death to Gentile Christians of Paul's churches in Asia in general, as a statement of his teaching. On this view the question of its destination hardly matters.

outline: Greeting: Paul, the saints, grace and peace
The great blessing: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed
Paul's prayer: to know God, and the power that raised Christ
From death to life: saved by grace through faith
Jew and Gentile: one new humanity, one household, one temple
The mystery made known: Paul's task for the Gentiles
Paul's prayer for strength and love, and the doxology
One body: unity and the gifts of Christ
The old way and the new: light and darkness
The household: wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters
The armor of God: standing against the powers

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Ephesians against Ephesus and the province of Asia: the temple of Artemis, magic and emperor worship, the Jewish community and its rights, Paul in prison (Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus), the Roman household and the household codes. Clinton Arnold's study of the powers in Ephesians is an example.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made: whether Paul wrote it or a follower did, the relation to Colossians, the missing words 'in Ephesus', the unusual style and vocabulary, the textual history, and the claims of the letter about itself. Lincoln, Best and Schnackenburg take the critical side on authorship; Hoehner, Arnold, Thielman and Barth defend Paul.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the shape of the letter: the long sentences of 1:3-14 and 1:15-23, the prayer reports and doxology, the pattern 'once... but now', the compounds with 'together', the images of body, building and household, and the household code and the armor image of the second half.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Ephesians as a letter from a Jew to Gentiles about Israel's gifts: election, adoption, covenant, temple. Asks what 'the commonwealth of Israel', the dividing wall and the 'law of commandments' meant, and how the letter has been used in Christian replacement teaching and in Jewish-Christian dialogue.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows the letter through the churches: Chrysostom's homilies, Augustine, Calvin, Wesley, Irenaeus on recapitulation, and Catholic teaching on the church and on marriage as a sacrament (5:32).

sections.b:
Ephesians is a letter, but it does not read like a quarrel. Paul writes to Galatia in anger and to Corinth with many questions; here he writes with a long calm breath of praise and prayer. The first three chapters tell what God has done, and the last three what to do about it. The key phrase is 'in Christ' (and 'in him'), which appears dozens of times. The key words are given the same English each time: saints (God's holy people), redemption, mystery (a secret of God, now told), church (ekklesia), the heavenly world, fullness, grace, peace.

Read slowly. The first sentence runs 202 words in the Greek and the Plain English Translation breaks it at the natural steps; try reading it aloud as a prayer.

Chapters 1 to 3 are a blessing, a prayer, a teaching and a second prayer with a doxology. Chapters 4 to 6 begin 'I urge you', which marks the turn from what God has done to how to live. Many scholars point out that the letter's two halves each end in a doxology or a blessing, and that the same themes run through both: unity, the church, the powers, love, and the contrast of the old life and the new. The instructions on households (5:21-6:9) and the armor (6:10-20) belong to the second part of this book.

Ephesians and Colossians are close in wording and in themes. Both speak of redemption and forgiveness in Christ (Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:14), Christ as head of the body (Ephesians 1:22-23; 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18; 2:19), the mystery of Christ among the Gentiles (Ephesians 3:3-6; Colossians 1:26-27), believers raised with Christ (Ephesians 2:5-6; Colossians 2:12-13; 3:1), putting off the old self and putting on the new (Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:9-10), and the duties of wives, husbands, children, parents, slaves and masters (Ephesians 5:21-6:9; Colossians 3:18-4:1). Both send Tychicus in almost identical words (Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-8). The two letters also differ: Colossians answers a particular 'philosophy' (Colossians 2:8), Ephesians does not name any rival teaching; Colossians writes of Christ as head of the powers (Colossians 2:10), Ephesians of the church as the place where their defeat is seen (3:10).

Three explanations are given. The same author wrote both within weeks, and the repetitions are natural. A disciple took Colossians as a model and expanded it (Lincoln). Or the two were drafted together by Paul and a co-worker. Colossians is not yet on this site; compare it when it is added.

Ephesus was the greatest city of Asia and the home of the temple of Artemis, counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Acts shows a city in which a silversmiths' guild lived off the goddess (Acts 19:23-41), in which magical books were worth a fortune (Acts 19:19) and in which Jews, 'God-fearers' and pagans lived side by side. Clinton Arnold has argued that the language of 'rulers, authorities, powers and lordships' in Ephesians (1:21; 3:10; 6:12) speaks to this world of spirits, spells and fate. If the letter was meant to be read by churches across Asia, the same picture held across the province, where emperor worship and local gods were everywhere. The notes on 1:21, 2:2 and 3:10 draw on this. The topic page on the powers gives the views.

sections.h: Jews and Gentiles: the heart of the first half
sections.b: The letter's central topic is not private salvation but the relation of Gentiles to Israel. Gentiles were 'cut off from the commonwealth of Israel' and 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' (2:12); now they are 'citizens together with the saints' and 'heirs together' (2:19; 3:6). A reader should keep three things in mind. First, Paul is writing as a Jew, and the gifts he lists in 1:3-14 (chosen, adopted, redeemed, inheritance) belong to Israel before they belong to the nations. Second, the letter never says that Israel has been replaced. Third, in the history of Christian teaching, passages like 2:15 ('the law of commandments... put out of effect') have been used against Jews. Catholic teaching since Vatican II cites Ephesians 2:14-16 to say that Christ reconciled Jews and Gentiles and made both one (Nostra Aetate 4), and many scholars today read the letter as an account of how Gentiles are brought in, without saying that the Jews' calling has ended. The card on 3:6 gives the positions of the churches.

The text is in good shape, with one large exception: the words 'in Ephesus' in 1:1 are absent from P46 (a papyrus of Paul's letters from about AD 200), from the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 300s), from Minuscule 1739 and from a corrector of Minuscule 424, and Basil of Caesarea (Against Eunomius 2.19) says that he found them absent in old copies. Marcion's collection called the letter 'to the Laodiceans' (Tertullian, Against Marcion 5.11, 5.17). The Byzantine text differs from the SBLGNT at several places (1:1, 1:14, 2:15, 2:17, 3:3, 3:9, 3:14, 3:21); these are given as variants. The notes use the SBLGNT and the Byzantine text printed in this site's source texts, and name manuscripts only where a page that was opened lists them.

Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the Ephesian church and said that Paul mentions the Ephesians in every letter (To the Ephesians 12:2). Polycarp echoes the letter and perhaps cites it as Scripture, and Irenaeus drew on 1:10 for his doctrine of recapitulation (Against Heresies 3.16.6). Chrysostom preached 24 homilies on it; Calvin wrote a commentary on it; Wesley's sermon on 2:8 is one of his main statements of salvation. The Catholic Catechism cites 5:32 in its teaching on marriage as a sacrament (Catechism 1616); the Reformation churches make 2:8-9 a motto of grace. Its picture of the church as body, bride and temple has shaped nearly every Christian doctrine of the church, as the book-wide card shows.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Ephesians as a letter written to be read at a baptism
spec.body: The shape of the letter may fit a baptismal occasion. Chapters 1 and 2 say what happens to a person in Christ: blessed, chosen, sealed with the Spirit (1:13), raised with Christ from death (2:5-6). Chapter 4 speaks of putting off the old self and putting on the new (4:22-24), chapter 5 has a call to the sleeper to wake and rise, apparently from a hymn (5:14), a washing of the church by water with the word (5:26), and 'one baptism' (4:5). The moves of the prayers (kneel, be strengthened, be rooted) and the doxology also sound like a worship service. If the letter was a teaching read to those about to be baptized, or newly baptized, in Gentile churches in Asia, the repeated 'you were... but now you are' (2:1-13; 5:8) would be the account of their own change. This overlaps with older proposals of a baptismal or liturgical setting and with the baptismal readings of Colossians and 1 Peter. The evidence is thin: the letter does not mention a ceremony beyond 'one baptism', and nothing proves the readers were newly baptized.
spec.refs: Ephesians 1:13; Ephesians 2:5-6; Ephesians 4:5; Ephesians 4:22-24; Ephesians 5:8; Ephesians 5:14; Ephesians 5:26

prompts: A Gentile house church in Ephesus in lamplight: a dozen men, women, children and a slave, sitting on mats in a modest courtyard, listening as a reader unrolls a very long scroll of papyrus, line after line, that falls across his knees and onto the floor like a river of ink. Behind them, over the rooftops, the pale marble temple of Artemis with its many columns glows in the dusk. Sketched by hand onto old rolled parchment mixed with cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor washes; wobbling ink lines, torn edges; no hard rectangular frame.

A great stone barrier with carved Greek letters, cracked in the middle, and through the gap walk two groups of people in different clothes, some in Jewish prayer shawls and some in Greek tunics, holding each other's hands. Over them, a simple lamp. Drawn in the style of an ancient manuscript illumination with cave-drawing figures and fading watercolor edges; rough parchment; soft borders, no sharp frame.
Seated with Christ in the heavenly world

A small human figure on a woven mat in a room of the ancient world, and above the roof beams a bright opening in the sky where a larger seated figure is shown in a simple robe with a luminous ring, in the manner of an early icon; between them a line of lamps. Sketched onto a scroll with ochre and charcoal, cave painting marks mixed with modern wash; edges soft and torn.

traditions.q: What is the church, according to the churches (1:22-23; 2:19-22)?
views: The one church of Christ, his body, is a visible society with bishops in the succession of the apostles under the pope, and a spiritual community at once. The Second Vatican Council taught that this church 'subsists in' the Catholic Church, while elements of sanctification and truth are found outside its visible limits (Lumen Gentium 7-8).

The church is the Body of Christ, one, holy, catholic and apostolic, living in every local church gathered round its bishop at the Eucharist. The Orthodox church holds that its life is the continuation of the apostles'.
The church is the assembly of all believers among whom the gospel is purely taught and the sacraments are rightly given; for true unity it is enough to agree on that (Augsburg Confession VII).

There is a universal church that is invisible and made up of all the elect of all ages, and visible churches in which the word is preached and the sacraments administered (Westminster Confession 25.1-2; Belgic Confession 27-29).

The visible church of Christ is a congregation of 'faithful men' (the Article's words) in which the pure Word of God is preached and the sacraments are duly ministered (Article 19); the Lambeth Quadrilateral of 1888 names the historic episcopate among four points.

The church is a local congregation of baptized believers who govern themselves under Christ; in a wider sense it is the whole company of the redeemed of all ages (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 6).

reading: Andrew T. Lincoln, Ephesians (Word Biblical Commentary 42, 1990)
A commentary that takes the letter as written by a disciple after Paul's death.
Harold W. Hoehner, Ephesians: An Exegetical Commentary (2002)
A major commentary that defends Paul as author.
Ernest Best, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on Ephesians (International Critical Commentary, 1998)
A commentary that argues the letter was not written by Paul.
Clinton E. Arnold, Ephesians: Power and Magic (1989) and Ephesians (Zondervan Exegetical Commentary, 2010)
The most important study of the powers in Ephesians against the magic and religion of Ephesus.
A two-volume commentary that defends Paul as author.
Paul Trebilco, The Early Christians in Ephesus from Paul to Ignatius (2004)
A study of the early Christians in Ephesus.
A series of 24 homilies on the letter.
